# Data Used and Data Acquisition

This project used three main datasets to evaluate whether relative sea level rise and salinity trends are associated with potential ghost forest expansion in the Chesapeake Bay region. 

## Relative Sea Level Rise
The first dataset was relative sea level rise (RSLR) data from selected [NOAA Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services tide gauge stations](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/map/). Station metadata, including station name, latitude, and longitude, were retrieved using the [NOAA CO-OPS Metadata API](https://api.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/mdapi/prod/). Monthly mean sea level data were then downloaded through the [NOAA CO-OPS Data API](https://api.tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/api/prod/) using the `monthly_mean` water level product, the `MSL` datum, metric units, and a study period from 1994 through 2024. These data were used to estimate a linear RSLR trend in millimeters per year for each tide gauge station.

## Salinity
The second dataset was salinity monitoring data from the [Chesapeake Bay Program Water Quality DataHub](https://datahub.chesapeakebay.net/waterquality). The DataHub provides downloadable water quality monitoring records for the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries. For this project, salinity data were downloaded as CSV files for both mainstem and tributary monitoring stations, then loaded into Python from the local `Data` folder as `SalinityMain.csv` and `SalinityTributary.csv`. The two files were combined into one dataset, filtered to the `SALINITY` parameter, and cleaned by converting sample dates and measured values into usable formats. Stations were then filtered to keep only stations with at least five observations and recent data within the last five years of the dataset. A linear salinity trend was calculated for each remaining station in parts per thousand per year.

## Ghost Forest Pixel Proxy
The third dataset was land-cover data from the [USGS National Land Cover Database](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/eros/science/national-land-cover-database), specifically the NLCD land-cover layers for 2001 and 2021. NLCD provides spatially explicit land-cover classifications for the conterminous United States and is suitable for comparing land-cover change across multiple years. The NLCD data were retrieved directly in Python using the `nlcd_bygeom()` function from the [HyRiver/PyGeoHydro data retrieval tools](https://docs.hyriver.io/), which allowed the project to download NLCD data for a defined Chesapeake Bay bounding box. The bounding box used for the study area was `[-77.5, 36.5, -75.0, 40.0]`, corresponding to longitude and latitude limits around the Chesapeake Bay region. The downloaded NLCD layers were stored through the local cache file `Data/aiohttp_cache.sqlite`.

The NLCD land-cover data were used to identify potential ghost forest transition pixels. Pixels classified as forest in 2001 were selected using NLCD forest classes 41, 42, and 43, representing deciduous forest, evergreen forest, and mixed forest. Pixels classified as wetland in 2021 were selected using NLCD wetland classes 90 and 95, representing woody wetlands and emergent herbaceous wetlands. Pixels that were forest in 2001 and wetland in 2021 were treated as potential ghost forest transition areas. This approach does not prove that every selected pixel is a true ghost forest, but it provides a land-cover-based proxy for areas where forested land may have converted to wetland conditions over time.

After the three datasets were processed, they were converted into spatial datasets using `GeoPandas`. The NOAA tide gauge stations were used as the spatial anchor for the final analysis. A 15-kilometer buffer was created around each tide gauge station, and the analysis summarized the average salinity trend and the number of potential ghost forest transition pixels within each buffer. This produced the final comparison dataset used for the correlation analysis.
